chief_complaint: severe nausea, bloating, and early satiety after meals
hpi_details: A 59-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe nausea, bloating, and early satiety after meals. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his stomach is reacting badly to his high-dose diabetes tablets or that he has developed a simple stress-induced stomach ulcer.
concerns: He is worried that if he keeps throwing up his meals, his blood sugar will crash and cause him to pass out while operating machinery at work.
expectations: He hopes to receive an effective anti-nausea medication so he can keep his meals down and manage his diabetes properly.
pmh: Long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy, poorly controlled

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Diabetic Gastroparesis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes ordering a gastric emptying study and recommending small, frequent, low-fat meals with metoclopramide as needed, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe nausea, bloating, and early satiety after meals

Key HPI features: A 59-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe nausea, bloating, and early satiety after meals. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Diabetic Gastroparesis.
Relevant background/PMH: Long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy, poorly controlled
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Diabetic Gastroparesis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Gastric outlet obstruction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: signs of gastric outlet obstruction (succussion splash, persistent vomiting of old food), haematemesis or evidence of GI bleeding, severe dehydration, electrolyte derangement, or ketoacidosis from poor oral intake in a diabetic patient.
management_principles: Order gastric emptying study, recommend small frequent low-fat meals, metoclopramide
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of severe nausea, bloating, and early satiety after meals. HPI: delayed gastric emptying, diabetic neuropathy.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Diabetic Gastroparesis.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Diabetic Gastroparesis.
reference_soap.plan: Review medications and exclude mechanical obstruction, often with upper endoscopy or appropriate imaging, before gastric-emptying testing. Optimize glycemic control and recommend small, low-fat, low-fiber meals. Consider time-limited metoclopramide only when benefits outweigh neurologic adverse-effect risks.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Diabetic Gastroparesis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Diabetic Gastroparesis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Order gastric emptying study, recommend small frequent low-fat meals, metoclopramide

teaching.one_liner: Long-standing diabetes damages the nerves controlling stomach emptying, so food sits in the stomach too long, causing nausea, bloating, and feeling full after only a little food.
red_flags: Signs of gastric outlet obstruction (succussion splash, persistent vomiting of old food) — needs imaging/endoscopy to exclude mechanical obstruction
Haematemesis or evidence of GI bleeding
Severe dehydration, electrolyte derangement, or ketoacidosis from poor oral intake in a diabetic patient

must_ask.say: How long have you had diabetes, and how well controlled has it been?
Do you feel full after only eating a small amount?
Do you feel nauseous, or have you vomited undigested food from earlier meals?
Does the bloating get worse as the day goes on?
Have your blood sugar readings become harder to control or more unpredictable?
Do you have any numbness or tingling in your feet?

history.answer: I have been having terrible nausea, stomach fullness, and I feel completely stuffed after just a few bites of food.
These problems started about two months ago and have been getting steadily worse over time.
I feel nauseous after almost every meal, and I end up throwing up three or four times a week, usually an hour or two after eating.
When I vomit, it looks like undigested food that I ate hours earlier, with no blood, coffee-ground material, or green bile.
No, it is never projectile, and I do not wake up vomiting on an empty stomach in the morning.
I feel uncomfortable pressure and mild aching in my upper stomach, and throwing up relieves the fullness for a little while.
My stomach feels tight and bloated after meals, but I am still passing gas and my bowels move normally without diarrhea.
No, I have not had any fever or chills, and my wife ate the same food with me and is completely fine.
No, I have not had any headaches, neck stiffness, blurred vision, or confusion.
No, I have not hit my head or had any recent accidents.
I can still drink fluids, but my mouth feels quite dry and I notice I am urinating less often than usual.
I often feel thirsty, and lately my blood sugar readings have been swinging unpredictably between very high and surprisingly low.
No, I have not had any chest tightness, heart palpitations, or shortness of breath.
history.topic: Chest pain and shortness of breath

history.answer: I have not started any new medicines, I do not smoke marijuana or use drugs, and I only have a beer once in a while.
Yes, I have lost around eight pounds over the last two months because I get full so quickly.
No, I definitely do not induce vomiting or force myself to throw up.
I have had type 2 diabetes for about fifteen years, and my doctor told me my blood sugar has not been well controlled recently.
I can only eat three or four bites before feeling uncomfortably full, as if my stomach has no room left.
Yes, I have had numbness, tingling, and a burning sensation in both of my feet and toes for the past few years.
I figured my stomach is just reacting badly to my diabetes pills or that I've developed a simple stomach ulcer from stress.
I'm really worried that if I keep throwing up my meals, my blood sugar will crash while I'm operating heavy machinery at work.
I'm hoping to get some medicine to settle my stomach so I can eat properly again without feeling sick right away.
Besides diabetes and nerve problems in my feet, I have high blood pressure, but no history of stomach ulcers.
I had an appendectomy when I was twenty-five years old, but no other operations or hospital stays.
I take metformin pills twice a day, inject insulin each evening, and take a daily blood pressure pill.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink an occasional beer with friends, perhaps once or twice a month.
I work as an office accountant and live at home with my wife.
My father had type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure, and my mother had osteoarthritis.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Supine blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg with pulse 76 bpm, and standing blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg with pulse 86 bpm without dizziness.
Oral mucosa is slightly dry; no pharyngeal erythema, oral thrush, or tonsillar exudate.
Skin turgor is normal without tenting, and capillary refill time is under two seconds.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light, with normal extraocular movements and no nystagmus.
Neck is supple with full passive range of motion, and Kernig and Brudzinski signs are absent.
Abdomen is mildly distended and symmetric with a well-healed surgical scar in the right lower quadrant and no visible peristalsis.
Normoactive bowel sounds are present in all four quadrants, with no abdominal bruits and no succussion splash.
Tympanitic percussion note over the central abdomen with no shifting dullness.
Mild, diffuse tenderness is elicited in the epigastric region without guarding or abdominal rigidity.
No rebound tenderness is present in any quadrant.
Sensation to light touch and pinprick is diminished in a symmetric stocking distribution up to the mid-calf bilaterally.
Bilateral Achilles tendon reflexes are diminished, whereas patellar reflexes are preserved at 2+.
